bib.title: Controlled experiments on the web: survey and practical guide

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Controlled experiments on the web: survey and practical guide", Ron Kohavi, Roger Longbotham, Dan Sommerfield, Randal M. Henne (Microsoft). Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 18:140-181 (2009), DOI 10.1007/s10618-008-0114-1. Received 14 Feb 2008, accepted 30 Jun 2008, published online 30 Jul 2008.
COVERAGE: 110,961 of 110,961 chars, all 42 PDF pages (journal pp. 140-181) including abstract, sections 1-7, Appendix A and references. Nothing skipped. Text extracted cleanly. Figures were not viewed. Extraction file: /tmp/kohavi.txt (line numbers below refer to it).

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Minimum sample size per variant for 95% confidence and 80% power is n = 16 sigma^2 / Delta^2. Replace 16 by 21 for 90% power. A more conservative formula n=(4r sigma/Delta)^2 is from Wheeler 1974.
  number: 16 (80% power); 21 (90% power)
  setup: equal-sized variants, large-sample normal approximation, Delta = the change you want to detect.
  quote: "n = 16σ 2 /Delta12 (2)" ... "Replace the 16 by 21 in the formula above to increase the power to 90%."
  where: p.152, lines 450-466
- claim: Using conversion rather than revenue as the OEC cuts required sample size by 3.3x, from over 409,000 users to under 122,000. That turns about 6 weeks of runtime into about 2.
  number: 409,000 vs 122,000 users; factor 3.3
  setup: 5% of users purchase, spend about $75, average $3.75, sd $30. Goal is to detect a 5% change at 80% power.
  quote: "you will need over 409,000 users to achieve the desired 80% power" ... "you will need less than 122,000 users" ... "Using conversion as the OEC instead of purchasing spend can thus reduce the sample size required for the experiment by a factor of 3.3."
  where: p.153, lines 476-494
- claim: Sample size scales with the inverse square of the detectable effect. Detecting a 20% change instead of 5% needs 16x fewer users (7,600). A bug that drops the OEC by 20% in an experiment powered for 1% is detectable in 1/400 of the runtime.
  number: 7,600 users; 1/400 of runtime
  setup: conversion OEC, 5% baseline.
  quote: "the number of users needed drops by a factor of 16 to 7,600" ... "Such a bug can be detected not in 1/20th of the planned running time, but in 1/400th of the running time."
  where: p.153, lines 495-504
- claim: Filtering to users who actually reach the changed surface lowers variance. Analyzing only checkout starters needs 6,400 users, which is about 64,000 site visitors, versus 122,000 unfiltered.
  number: 6,400 checkout users; 64,000 total
  setup: 10% of users start checkout and 50% of those complete it. Goal is a 5% change.
  quote: "you will need only 6,400 users going through checkout to detect a 5% change"
  where: p.153, lines 505-517
- claim: A 50/50 split is most powerful. Runtime scales by about 1/(4p(1-p)), so a 99/1 split needs about 25x longer. Run at least a week or two, then in whole weeks, to capture day-of-week effects. A 99/1 test would need over 125 days, which is too long because of cookie churn.
  number: 25x; 125 days; 5 days at 50/50 becomes 25 days at 95/5
  setup: all else fixed. The 125-day example starts from a 5-day 50/50 minimum.
  quote: "if an experiment is run at 99%/1%, then it will have to run about 25 times longer than if it ran at 50%/50%." ... "should not be run at 99%/1% because it would require over 125 days"
  where: p.175-176, lines 1409-1438
- claim: Randomization needs three properties: equal assignment probability, consistency across visits, and no correlation between experiments. Optional extras are monotonic ramp-up and external control.
  number: none
  quote: "Repeat assignments of a single end user must be consistent" and "there must be no correlation between experiments."
  where: p.163-164, lines 900-923
- claim: Hash-and-partition tests found only MD5 free of cross-experiment correlation. SHA256 came close (needed a five-way interaction). Other hashes, including .NET's string hash, failed even a two-way interaction test. Seeding a PRNG per request induced correlations. Caching hashes and XORing them gave severe correlation between experiments.
  number: 5 simulated experiments, 1 million sequential user IDs
  setup: chi-square tests for interactions.
  quote: "found that only the cryptographic hash function MD5 generated no correlations between experiments. SHA256 (another cryptographic hash) came close, requiring a ﬁve-way interaction to produce a correlation."
  where: p.165, lines 981-990
- claim: Latency harms metrics. Amazon: +100ms gave -1% sales. Google: +500ms gave -20% revenue (second-hand, from a Marissa Mayer talk). Microsoft Live Search: +1s gave -1% queries per user and -1.5% ad clicks per user. +2s gave -2.5% and -4.4%.
  number: 1%, 20%, 1%/1.5%, 2.5%/4.4%
  setup: Linden 2006b; Mayer at Web 2.0; Kohavi 2007 (Live Search).
  quote: "slowed down by one second, queries per user declined by 1% and ad clicks per user declined by 1.5%; when the search results page was slowed down by two seconds, these numbers more than doubled to 2.5% and 4.4%."
  where: p.173, lines 1341-1352
- claim: Small UI changes can have order-of-magnitude effects. Doctor FootCare: variant A beat B by an order of magnitude, and the "upgrade" lost 90% of revenue. The coupon code field was the critical change. Microsoft Office help widget: replacing Yes/No with 5-star cut ratings by about 90%. A two-stage widget beat the single 5-star widget by 2.2x.
  number: 90%; 2.2x
  setup: Doctor FootCare example comes from Eisenberg 2003, not run by the authors. The Office help result is a Microsoft experiment.
  quote: "the site “upgraded” from the A to B and lost 90% of their revenue" ; "the number of ratings plummeted by about 90%" ; "by a factor of 2.2, i.e., the response rate was 2.2 times higher."
  where: p.143-144, lines 153-176
- claim: MSN home page ads: adding three offers lowered clickthrough by 0.38% (relative), p=0.02. The lost clicks were worth more than the expected ad revenue, so the idea was scrapped. Clicks were valued two ways, by destination-property value and by search-engine marketing replacement cost.
  number: 0.38% relative; p=0.02; 5% of MSN US users; 12 days
  setup: late 2007. Display Ads team estimated "tens of thousands of dollars per day" from the extra offers.
  quote: "A controlled experiment was run on 5% of the MSN US home page users for 12 days. Clickthrough rate decreased by 0.38% (relative change), and the result was statistically significant (p-value = 0.02)."
  where: p.146, lines 217-221
- claim: Amazon Behavior-Based Search (a backend algorithm change) raised revenue by 3%, which was "several hundreds of millions of dollars". This is second-hand, from an April 2006 UW iEdge Seminar talk by Amazon. Amazon's shopping-cart recommendations (Linden) won an experiment despite a senior VP's opposition.
  number: 3%
  quote: "the feature increased Amazon’s revenue by 3%, which translates into several hundreds of millions of dollars."
  where: p.148, lines 259-261
- claim: Cited ROI anecdotes from Forrester, all second-hand, none verified by the authors. Marriott +$30M bookings. Coach search +200%. Iomega campaign yield +50%. InterContinental +$45M-$60M. Amtrak: 1 in 4 registration attempts succeed, and +20% registrations would add over $15M/year.
  number: $30M; 200%; 50%; $45M-$60M; $15M/year
  quote: "Marriott realized an additional $30 million in bookings with a new online reservations form."
  where: p.148, lines 270-289
- claim: Robots that accept cookies bias the comparison and inflate variance. Examples run to 7,000 clicks in an hour or over 3,000 page views a day. Filter them aggressively. Robots can produce much more than 5% false positives in A/A tests.
  number: 7,000 clicks/hour; 3,000 page views/day; 5% A/A false-positive rate
  quote: "we have found some robots that have up to 7,000 clicks on a page in an hour or more than 3,000 page views in a day."
  where: p.155-156, lines 574-614
- claim: Run continuous A/A tests. Check that users split as planned, that data matches the system of record, and that results are non-significant 95% of the time. Ramp up gradually (e.g. 0.1% to 0.5% to 2.5% to 10% to 50%) and auto-abort a failing treatment.
  number: 0.1% -> 0.5% -> 2.5% -> 10% -> 50%
  quote: "Are the results showing non-significant results 95% of the time?" / "An auto-abort simply reduces the percentage of users assigned to the underperforming Treatment to zero."
  where: p.174-175, lines 1381-1398; p.156, lines 618-627
- claim: Confidence intervals. Absolute effect is diff +/- 1.96*sigma_d. Percent effect uses Fieller's interval. Do not compute it if the CI of the denominator contains zero. Percent change is more intuitive: a CTR effect of 0.00014 was a 12.85% change.
  number: 1.96; 0.00014 = 12.85%
  quote: "the treatment effect for speciﬁc clickthrough rate was 0.00014. This translated to a 12.85% change due to the Treatment."
  where: p.154-155, lines 526-573
- claim: Choose the OEC in advance (a planned comparison), to avoid familywise type I error. Prefer a single metric. It should include long-term predictors (lifetime value, repeat visits), not just clicks. Multiple-comparison corrections lower power.
  number: none
  quote: "it is important to decide in advance on the OEC (a planned comparison); otherwise, there is an increased risk of ﬁnding what appear to be signiﬁcant results by chance"
  where: p.154, lines 518-525; p.150, lines 350-361; p.176, lines 1443-1456
- claim: "No significant difference" does not mean "does not hurt". The test may be underpowered. A significant but tiny gain may not justify maintenance cost.
  number: none
  quote: "It is possible that the experiment is negative but underpowered."
  where: p.176, lines 1457-1468
- claim: Software migrations can be tested as A/B with the goal of retaining the null. This needs enough power. The authors saw migrations declared complete that an A/B test showed to differ on key metrics.
  number: none
  where: p.156, lines 638-646
- claim: MVT options. Full factorial of 5 factors = 2^5 = 32 groups. An 8-group fractional factorial gives main effects but confounds all interactions. Estimating all two-factor interactions of 5 factors needs 16 combinations. The authors prefer concurrent independently randomized one-factor tests (a full factorial in the end) or overlapping experiments. Power is the same for a main effect regardless of the number of cells if the analysis pools all data. Power drops with more levels per factor or a treatment share under 50%. Their experience is that large interactions are rarer than people believe. The first experiment should be an A/B test.
  number: 32 groups; 8 groups; 16 combinations; 5 factors in 1 month vs 5 months
  quote: "You cannot estimate any interactions well with this design since all interactions are totally confounded with main effects or other two-factor interactions."
  where: p.158-163, lines 700-891
- claim: Assignment methods compared. Traffic splitting (non-intrusive, high hardware cost, suits platform migrations). Page rewriting (proxy; hard for https, backend and encrypted checkout pages). Client-side JavaScript (the third-party tool model; adds render latency; the "skip the call for Control" optimization is incorrect because it correlates latency with assignment). Server-side API (most general, intrusive, transparent to users; can be tied to a CMS, as in Amazon's slots). Service-based data collection is the preferred data path.
  number: none (Table at p.171)
  quote: "This optimization is incorrect (and should not be used) because it causes the render time delay to become correlated with variant assignment"
  where: p.166-173, lines 1013-1319
- claim: Event-triggered filtering restricts analysis to users, and to the portion of behavior, actually affected by the experiment, by tracking when each user first saw the affected content.
  number: none
  where: p.171-172, lines 1267-1281
- claim: Randomizing by user ID fails in some cases, so randomize items or pages instead. Examples: eBay first-bidder incentive (the treatment affects all items); price elasticity (Amazon's price test angered customers in 2000); SEO and robot tests (robots set no cookies).
  number: none
  where: p.178-179, lines 1536-1568
- claim: Controlled experiments establish causality because random assignment neutralizes confounders. Post-hoc analysis and interrupted time series (quasi-experiments) do not. Data-mining patterns are correlational.
  number: none
  quote: "Controlled experiments neutralize confounding variables by distributing them equally over all values through random assignment"
  where: p.142, lines 95-98; p.177, lines 1494-1500

LIMITS (authors' section 3.6 plus others)
- Metrics only, no "why". Qualitative methods are needed alongside.
- Short-term focus. Typical runs are a few weeks, so long-term goals must be built into the OEC, including latent conversions.
- Primacy and newness (Hawthorne) effects. Run multiple weeks, or analyze new users only.
- The feature must be implemented to production quality.
- Consistency. A user on several devices or cookies may see several variants.
- Parallel experiments. The authors claim interactions are rare and say pairwise tests can flag them. This is an assertion, not shown.
- Launch events and media announcements require all users to see the feature.
- Cookie-based user ID assumptions. Cookie churn contaminates long runs. Cookie-less users are excluded.
- The authors take it as given that sample sizes are large enough for the CLT, and assume independent units.
- Dated: the tooling is from 2008 (Google Website Optimizer, Offermatica, Optimost, SiteSpect). Many ROI examples are second-hand anecdotes. The paper does not cover sequential testing and peeking, SRM (sample ratio mismatch) by name, variance reduction like CUPED, network interference or spillover (only the Appendix A cases), or Bayesian methods. Multi-armed bandits are mentioned in one line only. The conversion-rate and sample-size examples use the rule-of-thumb 16 sigma^2/Delta^2, not an exact power calculation.
- Terminology slip: it defines "Confidence level" as the probability of failing to reject when H0 is true. Wheeler's formula is flagged as approximate and conservative.

BUILDS ON: Box, Hunter and Hunter 2005; Mason, Gunst and Hess 1989; Keppel et al. 1992; Roy 2001 (OEC); van Belle 2002 (16 sigma^2/Delta^2); Wheeler 1974; Fieller (via Willan and Briggs 2006); Plackett and Burman 1946; Davies and Hay 1950; Weiss 1997; Rossi et al. 2003; Linden 2006a,b; Kohavi et al. 2004; Kohavi 2007 (eMetrics talk); Peterson 2004, 2005; Eisenberg 2003-2005; Thomke 2003; Maron and Moore 1994 (Hoeffding races).

CODE: none in the paper. Key formulas, verbatim: "t = OB − OA / σ̂d (1)"; "n = 16σ 2 /Delta12 (2)"; "CI Limits = OB − OA ± 1.96 ∗ σ̂d (4)"; "Pct Diff = (OB − OA)/OA ∗ 100% (5)"; Fieller interval (6) is at lines 562-570. The runtime multiplier at non-50/50 splits is "1 /(4p(1 − p)".

FIGURES (not viewed; captions from text)
- Fig 1 (p.143): Doctor FootCare checkout, variant A vs B (shows the coupon-code effect).
- Fig 3/4 (p.145): Office help widgets, two-stage vs 5-star.
- Fig 5 (p.146): MSN home page, Control vs proposed treatment.
- Fig 6 (p.147): Amazon search for "24" with and without BBS.
- Fig 7 (p.149): high-level A/B flow, 100% users split 50/50 into Control and Treatment, instrumented and analyzed. This is the fastest intro diagram.
- Tables 1-2 (pp.161-162): fractional factorial (8 groups) and Plackett-Burman (12 groups) designs for 5 factors.
- Table at p.171: comparison of assignment methods.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. A fontTools warning at extraction is harmless. Equation (2) extracted garbled as "/Delta12". Table 1 and 2 sign columns lost their spacing. Section 3.5.1 is cross-referenced in section 6.2.2 as "Sect. 3.3" (the paper's own mislabel). In 2.1 the text cites "Fig. 2" where it means Fig. 1 or the follow-up variant.
